common_name: Marquette Grape (Extreme Cold-Hardy Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun once soil is workable.

directions: Marquette is a University of Minnesota-bred red wine grape descended in part from Pinot Noir, valued for surviving winter lows near -30°F with only minor cane damage. Vines are vigorous and require an early, thorough trellis training program along with cluster thinning to manage heavy fruit set. The grapes produce a deeply colored, medium-bodied red wine with notes of black cherry, black pepper, and spice, and the variety shows good resistance to downy mildew though it can be prone to black rot in humid seasons. Site vines with good air circulation and avoid low frost pockets to protect the early-breaking buds from late spring freezes.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Frontenac Grape (Cold-Hardy Riparia-Derived Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Set dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun in early spring; space rows to allow good airflow.

directions: Frontenac was released by the University of Minnesota from a Landot 4511 by Vitis riparia cross, and its riparia parentage gives it exceptional hardiness to roughly -35°F, making it a mainstay for upper-Midwest and Canadian vineyards. The vine is vigorous, productive, and reliably winter-hardy without hilling, but the fruit carries very high natural acidity that typically needs to be balanced through deacidification or blending during winemaking. Berries are small, black, and produce a deep ruby wine with cherry and dried-cranberry character; the foliage also colors attractively red-purple in autumn. Prune to a bilateral cordon or cane system and thin fruit clusters in high-vigor years to concentrate flavor.

common_name: La Crescent Grape (Cold-Hardy Aromatic White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring on a trellis in full sun with well-drained soil.

directions: La Crescent is a University of Minnesota-bred white wine grape prized for its intensely aromatic fruit, with apricot, citrus, and honeysuckle notes reminiscent of Muscat and Riesling. It shares the extreme cold-hardiness of its Minnesota-bred siblings, tolerating winter lows near -30°F, but ripens its fruit with very high sugar and high acid simultaneously, which winemakers use to produce off-dry or dessert-style wines. The compact clusters are prone to bunch rot in wet years, so growers benefit from leaf pulling around the fruit zone to improve airflow and sun exposure. Vigorous shoot growth means canopy management and cluster thinning are needed to avoid overcropping thin canes.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Traminette Grape (Cornell-Bred Aromatic White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun once the ground can be worked in spring.

directions: Traminette was developed at Cornell University from a cross of Gewürztraminer with the French-American hybrid Joannes Seyve 23.416, combining Gewürztraminer's spicy floral aroma with much better cold tolerance and disease resistance than its vinifera parent. The vine buds out relatively late, which helps it dodge spring frosts, and it is widely planted across the mid-Atlantic, Midwest, and Northeast for its lychee, rose, and clove-scented white wine. It shows good resistance to powdery mildew and moderate resistance to bunch rot compared with straight vinifera cultivars, though crop loads should still be managed through cluster thinning for wine quality. Train on a vertical shoot-positioned trellis and prune to spurs or short canes for consistent yields.

common_name: Chambourcin Grape (Disease-Resistant French-American Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Set dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun in spring, choosing a site with a long frost-free season.

directions: Chambourcin is a French-American hybrid bred by Joannes Seyve that has become a signature red wine grape of Missouri, Pennsylvania, and other humid eastern growing regions because of its strong natural resistance to downy and powdery mildew. It is a late-ripening variety that needs a fairly long, warm growing season to fully mature, so it is less suited to the shortest-season northern climates than Minnesota-bred hybrids. The wine is deeply colored with soft tannins and fruity black-cherry and berry character, and can be produced in styles ranging from light and fruity to full-bodied and oak-aged. Canopy management to expose fruit clusters helps color and ripeness given its late harvest window.
sources: Missouri State University Grape and Wine Institute

common_name: Chancellor Grape (Historic French-American Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun in early to mid spring.

directions: Chancellor, originally bred in France as Seibel 7053, was one of the most widely planted French-American red hybrids in the eastern United States through the mid-20th century, prized for its reliable productivity and moderate winter hardiness. The grape ripens midseason into loose clusters of blue-black berries that yield a soft, fruity red wine, historically used both as a varietal and as a blending grape to add color and body. It is more susceptible to bunch rot in wet years than the newer Minnesota-bred hybrids, so growers should prioritize good air circulation and timely fungicide applications during fruit set. Cane- or cordon-train on a vertical trellis and moderate crop loads to concentrate flavor in the smaller clusters.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in very acidic, well-drained soil in full sun in early spring.

directions: Northsky is one of the most compact of the University of Minnesota half-high blueberries, growing only 10 to 18 inches tall, which makes it well suited to foundation plantings, containers, and rock-garden-style edible landscapes in severe-winter regions. It shares the extreme cold-hardiness of its half-high siblings, tolerating temperatures near -35°F when snow-covered, and ripens medium-sized, light-blue, sweet berries in mid- to late summer. Because the plant is so low-growing, mulching and consistent moisture are especially important to prevent root stress during dry spells. Plant alongside another half-high cultivar such as Northblue or Polaris to improve pollination and fruit set.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in very acidic, well-drained soil in full sun in early spring.

directions: Chippewa is a later University of Minnesota half-high release valued for combining a compact, 2- to 3-foot habit with unusually large berries for a half-high type and an early-to-midseason ripening window. It tolerates winter lows to roughly -30°F and performs reliably in zones where standard highbush blueberries suffer dieback, while still producing fruit with good sweetness and firm texture. Like other half-high cultivars it needs highly acidic soil, so growers should test pH and amend with elemental sulfur before planting if needed. Cross-pollinate with a second half-high or highbush cultivar to maximize berry size and yield.
